paper_metadata.title: Quantum Computing for Supply Chain Finance

summary: The paper evaluates VQE and QAOA for supply‑chain finance portfolio optimization over 10 companies with 20 financial features, selecting 6 assets under a risk parameter q∈[0,1]. On noiseless Qiskit simulators, the classical minimum‑eigenvalue solver achieved higher average accuracy (0.5667) than VQE (0.4467) and QAOA (0.4183), and ANOVA shows no statistically significant difference (F(2,15)=0.9649, p=0.403).

experiments.description: Portfolio optimization for supply chain finance using a classical minimum-eigenvalue solver, VQE, and QAOA on IBM Qiskit simulators; evaluated by matching selected companies against an underwriter's manual selections across risk levels q=0.0 to 1.0.

algorithm.variant: classical minimum-eigenvalue algorithm, VQE, and QAOA applied to mean-variance portfolio optimization

hyperparameters.budget_constraint: number of selected companies equals budget B; all financing amounts assumed equal

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Binary decision variable x_i indicates whether company i is selected for financing (x_i=1) or not (x_i=0); problem mapped from mean-variance portfolio optimization to a Hamiltonian via a penalty term enforcing the budget constraint.
problem_formulation.objective_function: min q x^T Σ x - μ^T x, with equality constraint 1^T x = B enforced via penalty term (1^T x - B)^2; q controls risk appetite.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Penalty term (1^T x - B)^2 scaled by a parameter and subtracted from the objective; budget constraint requires selecting exactly B companies.
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: Hamiltonian corresponding to the penalized mean-variance objective; exact operator form not explicitly given in the paper.

problem_instance.description: Trade finance / supply chain finance portfolio selection over 10 companies from retail and steel sectors, geographically diversified.

dataset_specification.preprocessing: 20 performance parameters collected from annual reports, quarterly filings, manual underwriting, and country risk evaluation; weighted and summed into a score.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Performance parameters were mapped to values between 0 and 100, weighted by relative importance, and summed in Microsoft Excel; covariance computed in Python/NumPy; interest rate used as equivalent return.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: For each q in {0.0,0.1,...,1.0}, algorithm selections were compared to manual underwriter selections; accuracy score computed as number of matching selections. Additional analysis reduced selection count from 6 to 1 and reran experiments across all q values. One-way ANOVA used to compare distributions.

implementation_details.classical_solver: Microsoft Excel, Python/NumPy, and IBM Qiskit classical optimizer interfaces
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Data extracted from Excel using Pandas; covariance computed with NumPy; weighted scores calculated in Excel.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Accuracy scores and ANOVA computed from selection matches; results summarized across q values.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical minimum-eigenvalue algorithm / manual underwriter comparison
speedup_claims.conditions: on IBM Qiskit simulators for 10 companies, 20 features, q from 0.0 to 1.0
speedup_claims.caveats: Paper reports no statistically significant difference between VQE/QAOA and the classical algorithm (ANOVA p=0.403435); no quantum advantage observed.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not specified; experiments executed only on noiseless IBM Qiskit simulators without hardware resource estimates.
limiting_factors: Experiments performed only on noiseless simulators
Very small problem size (10 assets, 10 binary variables)
No circuit resource metrics reported (qubits, depth, shots)
No complexity analysis or asymptotic speedup claims
Classical minimum-eigenvalue solver achieves higher mean accuracy
Results compared to human underwriter heuristic rather than strong classical optimization benchmark

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_other because the paper states all experiments were executed on quantum simulators and no specific simulator backend or QPU device is named.
Num qubits not explicitly stated; inferred problem size is 10 binary variables from selecting among 10 companies, but actual circuit register size is not reported.
The paper explicitly states no statistically significant difference and no advantage seen from quantum algorithms, supporting speedup_order='none'.

The paper uses Qiskit tutorials and IBM Quantum network simulators; VQE and QAOA are the gate-based quantum experiments, while the classical minimum-eigenvalue algorithm is a baseline within the same experiment.
Discussion explicitly states there is no statistically significant difference between classical and quantum algorithms (ANOVA F(2,15)=0.96, p=0.40).
Table III shows classical average accuracy 0.5667 vs VQE 0.4467 and QAOA 0.4183, indicating classical performs slightly better.
Therefore parity or slight classical advantage is observed rather than quantum advantage.
